body_markdown:
Cervical screening is one of the most effective ways to prevent cervical cancer, yet many eligible women in the UK do not attend their appointments. Concerns about discomfort, embarrassment, privacy, time and previous negative experiences can all make it harder for people to take part.


A new NHS approach aims to remove some of those barriers by offering eligible women the opportunity to test for human papillomavirus, commonly known as HPV, at home. The programme is expected to make screening more convenient for people who have missed appointments and could help identify those who need further checks.


According to figures reported by NHS England, only 68.8 per cent of eligible women are currently up to date with cervical screening. The national target is 80 per cent, highlighting the gap between the number of people invited for screening and those who actually take part.


The NHS plans to offer millions of women free home testing kits over the coming year.


## What is an HPV home test?


An HPV home test is designed to allow someone to collect a sample themselves rather than attending a clinic initially.


The kit contains a swab that is used to collect a vaginal sample. Once the sample has been collected, it is returned to an NHS laboratory, where it is tested for high-risk types of HPV.


The important point is that the home test is primarily looking for HPV, rather than directly examining cervical cells for abnormalities.


If high-risk HPV is detected, the person will generally be asked to attend a healthcare appointment for conventional cervical screening or further assessment. A clinician can then collect cells from the cervix and determine whether there are any changes that may require monitoring or treatment.


This means a home HPV test should be viewed as an alternative way into the screening pathway, rather than a complete replacement for every stage of cervical screening.


## What exactly is HPV?


Human papillomavirus refers to a large group of viruses. HPV is extremely common and can be transmitted through sexual contact. Many infections cause no noticeable symptoms and clear naturally, while some types can cause genital warts.


Other types are classified as high risk because persistent infection can cause changes in cells that may eventually develop into cancer.


HPV is strongly associated with cervical cancer. Cancer Research UK reports that almost all cases of cervical cancer are linked to persistent infection with high-risk HPV.


Importantly, having HPV does not mean that someone has cancer. In many cases, the immune system clears the infection without treatment. Screening is valuable because it can identify people who may need closer monitoring before serious cell changes develop.


## Who is being offered a home testing kit?


The programme is intended particularly for women who are not up to date with cervical screening.


According to the information reported on 26 August 2026, invitations are being sent to eligible women aged between 30 and 65 who have missed screening. Invitations may arrive by letter, email, text message or through the NHS app.


Those who receive an invitation can use the instructions provided to request a kit.


The programme is also intended to improve participation among groups that may face additional barriers to attending screening. These can include people with disabilities, some ethnic minority communities and LGBT+ people, alongside anyone who finds traditional appointments difficult or uncomfortable.


Eligibility can depend on individual circumstances and the screening programme operating in the relevant part of the UK, so people should follow the instructions in their NHS invitation rather than assuming they qualify based solely on age.


## Why could home testing make a difference?


Traditional cervical screening usually involves a short appointment with a nurse or doctor. During the appointment, a speculum is used so that a soft brush can collect a sample of cells from the cervix.


Although the procedure is generally quick, some people find it uncomfortable or stressful. Others may struggle to attend because of work, childcare, transport, disability, anxiety or concerns about privacy.


A self-sampling option could remove some of these practical obstacles.


Research led by Queen Mary University of London, involving researchers including colleagues at King’s College London, has suggested that offering HPV self-testing could substantially increase screening participation and potentially prevent additional cases of cervical cancer.


The wider evidence also demonstrates the importance of screening. Cervical cancer rates in the UK have fallen significantly over the long term, with screening and HPV vaccination playing major roles in prevention.


## What happens if HPV is found?


A positive HPV result does not automatically mean cancer has been found.


Instead, it indicates that high-risk HPV has been detected and that further assessment may be needed. The next step can involve attending a healthcare professional for cervical screening.


During conventional screening, cells from the cervix can be collected and assessed when HPV is present. If abnormal cell changes are discovered, healthcare professionals can recommend appropriate monitoring or treatment.


This follow-up stage is important. Completing a home test but ignoring a request for further screening could mean that potentially important changes are not investigated.


## Why is cervical screening still important?


Cervical cancer can develop without obvious symptoms, particularly during its earlier stages. Screening aims to identify HPV and cell changes before cancer develops or while problems are still easier to manage.


The HPV vaccine has also transformed cervical cancer prevention. Vaccination protects against important HPV types responsible for many cervical cancer cases, but it does not eliminate the need for screening.


This is because the vaccine does not protect against every HPV type that can contribute to cancer, and screening provides another layer of protection.


Anyone who receives an invitation should therefore consider completing it, even if they have previously had the HPV vaccine.


## What should you do if you receive a kit?


Read the instructions supplied with the kit carefully and follow the collection and return process exactly as described.


If you have questions about your result, have difficulty collecting the sample or are unsure what to do next, contact the NHS service identified in your invitation or kit instructions.


Most importantly, a home test should not be used as a reason to ignore symptoms. Unusual vaginal bleeding, bleeding after sex, persistent unusual discharge, pelvic pain or other concerning symptoms should be discussed with a healthcare professional, even if a recent HPV test was negative.


### The bigger picture


The introduction of home HPV testing represents an attempt to make cervical cancer prevention more accessible. For people who have avoided or missed traditional appointments, being able to collect a sample privately at home could make screening feel more manageable.


However, the effectiveness of the programme will depend not only on people completing the home test, but also on ensuring that anyone with a positive result receives appropriate follow-up care.


For those invited, the simplest message is clear: do not ignore the invitation. Whether screening takes place through a traditional appointment or begins with a home HPV test, taking part can help identify risks before they develop into something more serious.


**Sources:** This article is based on information reported by *The Independent* on 26 August 2026, together with background information from NHS England and Cancer Research UK.


**Disclaimer:** This article is intended for general information only and is not medical advice. Eligibility, screening arrangements and NHS procedures can change, and programmes may operate differently across the UK. Always follow the instructions provided by the NHS and speak with a qualified healthcare professional about personal medical concerns or symptoms.
